lead: A power device dies when one of its limits is crossed, even for a microsecond. Ratings are those limits, printed on the datasheet as absolute maximum values. Protection keeps the device inside them: a snubber is a small R-C or L network beside the switch that slows the voltage and current edges, and a gate drive delivers a clean, isolated pulse to the gate. Phone chargers, inverters and 400 V traction drives use both.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for diode reverse recovery, Chapter 1.2 for SCR voltage and current ratings, and Chapter 1.6 for MOSFET and IGBT gate behaviour.

blocks.text: Absolute maximum ratings are values beyond which the device is damaged, not values at which it works well. A 600 V MOSFET run at 600 V fails; at 400 V it survives the overshoot every switching circuit produces.

Voltage ratings come in pairs. V<sub>DRM</sub> is the repetitive peak off-state voltage an SCR blocks every cycle; V<sub>DSM</sub> is the higher transient value it may survive once. For a MOSFET, V<sub>DSS</sub> is the drain-source breakdown; for a diode, V<sub>RRM</sub> is the reverse value.

Current ratings are average on-state current I<sub>T(AV)</sub> or I<sub>F(AV)</sub> at a stated case temperature, RMS current, repetitive peak current, and surge current I<sub>TSM</sub> — the single 50 Hz half-cycle current the device survives in a fault. The surge value falls as the pulse gets longer.

Two dynamic ratings decide protection. di/dt limits current rise at turn-on; in an SCR a fast rise turns on only a small patch near the gate and burns a hot spot. dv/dt limits off-state voltage rise; it drives current through junction capacitance and can turn an SCR or MOSFET on by itself. Gate charge Q<sub>g</sub> is the charge the driver supplies on every pulse.

Derating means running below the ratings. A common rule keeps steady voltage under 60–70 % of the blocking rating, current under 60–75 % of the rated value, and junction temperature at least 20 °C below Tj(max). Derating pays for overshoot, hot ambient and a cheap heat sink. Junction temperature is worked out in Chapter 1.8.

Series devices share voltage only if leakage and switching match; a resistor across each shares DC voltage, an R-C shares the transient. Parallel MOSFETs share current well because on-resistance rises with temperature, pushing current off the hotter device. BJTs and SCRs share poorly, since their on-state drop falls with temperature.
A snubber is a small network mounted close to the switch. It absorbs switching energy, slows one edge, and moves the loss into a resistor. It never removes loss.

The turn-off snubber is R<sub>s</sub> and C<sub>s</sub> in series across the switch. At turn-off the load current diverts into C<sub>s</sub>, so the switch voltage rises at dv/dt = I/C<sub>s</sub>. A larger C<sub>s</sub> slows the rise. The capacitor ends charged to the off-state voltage V. At the next turn-on it discharges through R<sub>s</sub> and the switch, and R<sub>s</sub> limits the peak discharge current to about V/R<sub>s</sub>.
E = ½ C<sub>s</sub> V²   and   P<sub>Rs</sub> = ½ C<sub>s</sub> V² f<sub>s</sub>
blocks.where: E is the energy stored in the snubber capacitor in joules; C<sub>s</sub> is its capacitance in farads; V is the off-state voltage across the switch in volts; f<sub>s</sub> is the switching frequency in hertz; P<sub>Rs</sub> is the average power dissipated in R<sub>s</sub> in watts when the capacitor is fully discharged once per cycle.

blocks.text: The resistor must carry this pulse power continuously, not its DC value. Place R<sub>s</sub> and C<sub>s</sub> with short leads at the switch terminals so the loop stays small.

The turn-on snubber is a series inductor L<sub>s</sub>. At turn-on it slows the current rise to di/dt ≈ V/L<sub>s</sub>. At turn-off the inductor current cannot stop instantly, so a freewheeling diode gives it a path; without that diode the switch sees a destructive voltage spike.

A gate driver turns a weak logic pulse into the current and voltage the gate needs. It must deliver the gate charge Q<sub>g</sub> quickly, give a clean edge, keep the power-side voltage away from the control side, and hold the gate firmly off when the switch must stay off.

Isolation is the first design choice. An optocoupler passes the pulse as light and gives several kilovolts of isolation, but it is slower and needs its own isolated supply. A pulse transformer is fast and cheap but cannot pass a DC level, so it suits narrow pulses. Isolated driver ICs with capacitive or magnetic barriers are common today.

blocks.where: I<sub>g,peak</sub> is the peak gate current in amperes; V<sub>drive</sub> is the driver supply voltage in volts; V<sub>GE</sub> is the gate-emitter voltage at the start of the pulse in volts; R<sub>g</sub> is the external gate resistor in ohms; R<sub>driver</sub> is the driver's internal resistance in ohms.

blocks.text: The gate resistor R<sub>g</sub> sets the switching speed. A small R<sub>g</sub> switches fast with low loss but gives high dv/dt, ringing and EMI. A large R<sub>g</sub> is quiet but slow and hot. Pick R<sub>g</sub> from the datasheet gate-charge curve, then check the waveform on the bench.

An IGBT in a bridge needs a negative off bias, typically −5 V to −8 V. When the opposite switch turns on, its rising collector voltage pushes Miller current through the gate-collector capacitance of the off device; that current raises the gate voltage, and without negative bias the IGBT can turn on and short the DC link. A negative bias plus a low-impedance turn-off path or a Miller clamp prevents this.

items: With the DC link off, apply a pulse train and check the gate-emitter voltage: negative when off, +15 V when on.
Measure the rise time and the peak gate current across R<sub>g</sub>; compare with Q<sub>g</sub> from the datasheet.
Run into a resistive load and check that turn-off overshoot stays under the derated voltage rating.
Repeat at full load and full temperature; look for gate ringing and false turn-on at the Miller plateau.

spec.aria: A gate driver sends pulses to a 400 V switch; a 10 nF capacitor with a series resistor is connected across the switch to absorb turn-off energy.

examples.question: A turn-off snubber has C<sub>s</sub> = 10 nF across a switch that blocks 400 V. The switching frequency is 20 kHz. Find the energy stored in C<sub>s</sub> at turn-off and the average power dissipated in R<sub>s</sub> if all that energy is lost once per cycle.
steps: C<sub>s</sub> = 10 nF = 10 × 10⁻⁹ F, V = 400 V, f<sub>s</sub> = 20 kHz = 20 × 10³ Hz.
R<sub>s</sub> must also limit peak discharge current to V/R<sub>s</sub>, and it needs a 16 W pulse rating, not a 2 W carbon resistor.
examples.answer: The snubber capacitor stores 0.8 mJ at turn-off, and R<sub>s</sub> must dissipate about 16 W.
examples.check:
C = 10e-9
V = 400.0
f = 20e3
E = 0.5 * C * V**2
P = E * f
print(round(E * 1000, 6))
print(round(P, 6))

traps: A snubber does not save energy. It moves loss from the switch to the resistor; total heat stays about the same.
C<sub>s</sub> without R<sub>s</sub> discharges through the switch at turn-on, limited only by stray resistance.
di/dt is a turn-on limit on current rise; dv/dt is an off-state limit on voltage rise. Do not swap them.
The snubber resistor needs a pulse rating at f<sub>s</sub>. A 5 W resistor fails at 16 W of pulses.
R<sub>g</sub> is not free: too small gives ringing and EMI, too large gives high switching loss and a hot device.

quiz.q: Name four datasheet ratings and what each one limits.
quiz.a: V<sub>DRM</sub> or V<sub>DSS</sub> limits blocked voltage; I<sub>TSM</sub> limits one 50 Hz half-cycle fault current; di/dt limits current rise at turn-on; dv/dt limits off-state voltage rise. Q<sub>g</sub> is the charge per pulse.

quiz.q: Why must a turn-off snubber capacitor have a series resistor?
quiz.a: At turn-off C<sub>s</sub> limits dv/dt. At the next turn-on it is charged to V and would dump that charge into the switch through near-zero resistance. R<sub>s</sub> limits discharge current to about V/R<sub>s</sub> and takes the energy as heat.

quiz.q: An R-C snubber with C<sub>s</sub> = 22 nF is connected across a switch blocking 500 V at 25 kHz. Find the energy per cycle and the power in R<sub>s</sub>.
quiz.a: E = ½ C<sub>s</sub> V² = 0.5 × 22 × 10⁻⁹ × 500² = 2.75 mJ. P = E f<sub>s</sub> = 2.75 × 10⁻³ × 25 × 10³ = 68.75 W. The resistor needs a pulse rating above this.

quiz.q: A technician removes R<sub>s</sub> from an R-C snubber to save the resistor loss. What happens at the next turn-on?
quiz.a: C<sub>s</sub> sits charged to the full off-state voltage. At turn-on it discharges through the switch with only stray resistance, so peak current and di/dt are very high and can exceed the ratings. The energy burns inside the switch instead of the resistor.

quiz.q: Compare a pulse transformer and an optocoupler as gate-drive isolation methods.
quiz.a: A pulse transformer is fast and cheap but passes no DC level, so it suits narrow pulses. An optocoupler transfers a DC level with kilovolts of isolation, but it is slower and needs an isolated gate supply.

quiz.q: A driver with a 15 V supply feeds a gate through R<sub>g</sub> = 10 Ω. The driver internal resistance is 5 Ω and the gate is at 0 V when the pulse starts. Find the peak gate current.
Why does an IGBT in a bridge need a negative gate bias when off?
quiz.a: When the opposite switch turns on, the off IGBT's collector voltage rises fast and drives Miller current through the gate-collector capacitance into the gate circuit. The gate voltage rises past threshold, turns the IGBT on, and shorts the DC link. A −5 V to −8 V bias and a low-impedance turn-off path keep the gate below threshold.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry designs snubbers and gate drives from the maker's switching-loss and gate-charge models, and proves them with a double-pulse test at real DC-link voltage and current. Active gate drives vary R<sub>g</sub> during the transient to trade dv/dt against loss. SiC and GaN devices switch so fast that the snubber is often replaced by a dv/dt filter at the terminals. Search next for 'double pulse test', 'Miller clamp', 'active gate drive' and 'SiC gate driver negative bias'. For converter-level design see Unit 3, DC-DC Converters.
